summary: A 1970 list of the Network Working Group notes numbered 1 to 80, compiled by J. B. North. It is an index.

eli5.summary: A table of contents for the first 80 notes.

questions: what were the first network rfcs about
when did the rfc series start
subtitle: An index and catalog of the first 80 network working group notes

tldr.problem: As the ARPANET community accumulated ideas, proposals, and discussions, researchers needed a way to find and reference earlier notes.
tldr.mechanism: J. B. North compiled an alphabetical listing of RFCs 1-80, showing the title, publication date, NIC number, and author for each note. The list shows which RFCs were actually issued and which were skipped or never published.
tldr.outcome: This index served as the first table of contents for the NWG archives, establishing the habit of cataloging network documentation.

today: RFC 84 is a historical index that has been superseded by modern RFC search tools and databases. However, it documents the ARPANET community's documentation practices and shows which early RFCs were deemed worth preserving. It is now a record of what the community prioritized in its first 18 months.

sections.title: The Index
sections.content: In December 1970, J. B. North compiled an index of all Network Working Group notes numbered 1 through 80. The index lists each RFC's number, publication date, NIC (Network Information Center) number, title, and author. It documents the rapid growth of the ARPANET community's written record, from the first note in April 1969 to RFC 80 in November 1970, spanning about 18 months.
sections.eli5: The RFC series started small, with one note every few weeks. By late 1970, there were 80 notes. Someone made a list so people could find them.

sections.title: What the List Reveals
sections.content: The index shows that some RFCs were never issued (such as 5, 14, and 26), suggesting editorial decisions to skip certain numbers or abandon proposals. The titles show the range of concerns: HOST software, documentation, protocol specifications, meeting notes, and hardware interfaces. Early RFCs often had cryptic titles or were cross-references. Frequent authors included Steve Crocker, Vint Cerf, and others from UCLA, reflecting the community's early clustering around a few centers.
sections.eli5: The list shows which notes were about protocols, which were about meetings, and which were skipped. Some people like Steve Crocker wrote a lot of notes.

sections.title: An Archive Emerges
sections.content: By creating this index, the NWG established a formal record and a numbering system that would persist. Unlike informal memos, numbered RFCs and NIC numbers made them citable and retrievable. The index itself has become a historical document, showing what the community was working on in the network's first year and a half, before many sites were even operational.
sections.eli5: Making a numbered list with a catalog number meant the notes were official records people could find and refer to later.
